title: Foundation Model Basics
summary: Definition and core characteristics of foundation models, including their pre-training on large datasets and ability to be adapted to various downstream tasks.
root: Introduction to Building AI Applications with Foundation Models
learning_objective: The learner can define foundation models and describe their core characteristics, including pre-training on large datasets and adaptability to downstream tasks.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing foundation models are immediately ready for specific applications without any adaptation or fine-tuning.
Assuming training a foundation model is a simple process rather than an incredibly complex and costly one.
Thinking you must know how to develop a foundation model from scratch to be able to use it effectively.

title: AI Application Architecture
summary: The structural components of AI applications built on foundation models, covering how models integrate with user interfaces, data pipelines, and external tools.
root: Introduction to Building AI Applications with Foundation Models
learning_objective: The learner can identify the structural components of AI applications built on foundation models, including how models integrate with user interfaces, data pipelines, and external tools.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing an AI application is only the foundation model itself, ignoring the surrounding UI, data pipelines, and tool integration layers.
Confusing the existence of a foundation model with the complete practice of AI engineering architecture.
Assuming the user interface is separate from or unimportant to the core AI application architecture.

title: User Feedback Integration
summary: Methods for collecting, processing, and incorporating user feedback to evaluate and improve AI application performance over time.
root: Introduction to Building AI Applications with Foundation Models
learning_objective: The learner can explain methods for collecting, processing, and incorporating user feedback to evaluate and improve AI application performance over time.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that simple thumbs up/down feedback alone is sufficient for deep analysis without additional context like dialogue turns.
Assuming that asking for positive feedback always clutters the interface or annoys users, ignoring that it can be managed by limiting frequency.
Thinking that acting on user feedback always improves the product, overlooking degenerate feedback loops that can amplify biases.

title: Self-Supervised Pre-training Objective
summary: Pre-training uses self-supervision on massive unlabeled text corpora, optimizing the model for text completion rather than conversation, which causes a pre-trained model to talk like a web page instead of a human.
learning_objective: The learner can explain how self-supervised pre-training infers labels from input text to optimize for text completion rather than conversation.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing self-supervised learning requires no labels at all, when it actually infers labels from the input data.
Assuming pre-training optimizes a model for human-like conversation rather than text completion.

title: Data Sources and Output Risks
summary: Pre-training data is often indiscriminately scraped from the internet, which can lead the model to produce outputs that are racist, sexist, rude, or factually wrong.
learning_objective: The learner can identify how indiscriminate internet scraping and AI-generated data introduce risks such as biased, rude, or factually wrong outputs, copyright violations, and benchmark contamination due to obscured data lineage.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that AI-generated data is inherently clean and free from the biases or errors present in the original training data.
Assuming that data lineage does not matter as long as the model performs well on benchmarks.
Thinking that training data extraction risks are limited to personally identifiable information and ignore copyrighted or common text regurgitation.

title: Pre-training as Parameter Compression
summary: Pre-training implicitly minimizes a model's intrinsic dimension, making larger models easier to finetune later with fewer trainable parameters and less data.
learning_objective: The learner can explain how pre-training acts as a compression framework by minimizing a model's intrinsic dimension, enabling more efficient fine-tuning with fewer parameters and less data.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that larger models have higher intrinsic dimensions after pre-training, when they actually tend to have lower ones.
Thinking pre-training only improves general performance rather than acting as a compression mechanism for downstream fine-tuning.
Assuming fine-tuning a pre-trained model requires training all parameters, ignoring that low intrinsic dimension allows for parameter-efficient methods.

title: Full Parameter Updates During Pre-training
summary: During pre-training, all model parameters are updated, in contrast to inference where no parameters are updated and finetuning where some or all may be updated.
learning_objective: The learner can state that during pre-training all model parameters are updated, distinguishing this from inference and finetuning.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that model parameters are updated during inference.
Assuming that finetuning always updates all model parameters like pre-training does.
Thinking that frozen parameters are updated during pre-training.

title: SFT vs Pre-training Objectives
summary: Explains how SFT shifts a model from generic text completion to conversational instruction-following using labeled instruction-response pairs.
learning_objective: The learner can explain how SFT shifts a model from generic text completion to conversational instruction-following using labeled instruction-response pairs.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing SFT is the same as pre-training rather than a post-training step that adapts a pre-trained model.
Thinking SFT requires reinforcement learning or human feedback to function.
Assuming SFT alone eliminates all harmful or incorrect outputs from a pre-trained model.

title: Next-Token vs Infilling Finetuning
summary: Describes the two SFT approaches: predicting the next token versus filling in blanks, with infilling being useful for text editing and code debugging.
learning_objective: The learner can distinguish between next-token and infilling finetuning and identify use cases where infilling is more suitable.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that a model must be pre-trained as a masked model to be finetuned for infilling.
Assuming infilling finetuning is exclusively for code debugging and not applicable to text editing.

title: Finetuning Frameworks and Compute
summary: Covers popular SFT frameworks such as LLaMA-Factory, PEFT, and Axolotl, and the compute requirements for full versus adapter-based finetuning.
learning_objective: The learner can compare full finetuning and adapter-based finetuning in terms of compute requirements and identify frameworks such as LLaMA-Factory, PEFT, and Axolotl for each approach.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing adapter-based finetuning is always faster than full finetuning regardless of model size or dataset.
Assuming all finetuning frameworks support identical methods and hardware configurations without trade-offs.
Thinking a mid-tier GPU is sufficient for full finetuning of most foundation models.

title: Preference Finetuning Objectives
summary: The goal of aligning model outputs with human preferences, the challenges of defining universal human preference mathematically, and the risks of over-censorship or misalignment.
learning_objective: The learner can explain the goal of preference finetuning and why capturing universal human preference mathematically is challenging.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that a single, universal human preference can be mathematically defined and embedded into AI.
Assuming preference-based feedback is always appropriate, even for questions that require factual correctness.
Thinking that more preference finetuning always improves a model without risking over-censorship or boring outputs.

title: Preference Data Collection
summary: The process of gathering human feedback to rank model outputs, creating datasets of preferred versus rejected responses for training.
learning_objective: The learner can describe how human feedback is collected to rank model outputs into preferred versus rejected response pairs for training preference models.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing all questions should be answered by preference rather than correctness, which can lead to misaligned behaviors.
Assuming users can reliably pick the correct answer when they lack the knowledge to evaluate the options.
Thinking human preference can be captured in a single mathematical formula.

title: Preference Optimization Algorithms
summary: Algorithms such as RLHF and DPO that optimize a model to generate responses matching human preferences based on ranked data.
learning_objective: The learner can explain how preference optimization algorithms such as RLHF and DPO use ranked human feedback to align model responses with user preferences.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing preference-based voting should be used for all questions, even those with objectively correct answers.
Assuming a single universal human preference exists and can be perfectly embedded into an AI model.

title: Domain Mix in Preference Finetuning
summary: How the optimal distribution of training domains, such as general knowledge, math, and coding, shifts during preference finetuning compared to earlier stages.
learning_objective: The learner can compare the optimal domain mix percentages for pre-training, supervised finetuning, and preference finetuning as shown in Table 8-1.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that the optimal distribution of training domains remains constant across all training phases.
Assuming that math and coding should continue to comprise nearly half of the training data during preference finetuning.

title: Data Quality
summary: The criterion ensuring training data is accurate, reliable, and free from errors, analogous to using fresh ingredients in cooking, which directly impacts model performance.
learning_objective: The learner can define data quality in model training and explain how high-quality data impacts model performance compared to noisy data.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that a larger volume of training data always leads to better model performance regardless of noise or relevance.
Assuming that data quality does not significantly affect model performance as long as the data quantity is sufficient.

title: Data Coverage
summary: The criterion ensuring the training data includes the right mix of domains and topics, such as general knowledge, math, coding, and multilingual content, without over- or under-representing any area.
learning_objective: The learner can explain data coverage as the criterion ensuring training data includes the right mix of domains and topics without over- or under-representing any area.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing data coverage is about the total amount of data rather than the diversity and balance of domains and topics.
Confusing data coverage with data quality, which concerns the correctness and reliability of individual examples rather than the mix of data.

title: Data Quantity
summary: The criterion determining the volume of training data required for a model, balancing the amount of data against training costs and desired capabilities.
learning_objective: The learner can explain how data quantity is determined by balancing training costs, desired capabilities, and the specific situation, recognizing that required amounts range from single examples to trillions of tokens.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that more data always leads to better performance regardless of quality or diversity.
Assuming there is a single fixed amount of data required for all models and tasks.
Thinking data quantity matters more than data quality and coverage for model performance.

title: Phase-Specific Data Mixes
summary: The variation in optimal data composition across different training phases, such as pre-training, supervised finetuning, and preference finetuning, as demonstrated by domain mix tables.
learning_objective: The learner can compare the optimal domain data mixes for pre-training, supervised finetuning, and preference finetuning using a domain mix table.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that the same data domain proportions are optimal across all training phases.
Assuming preference finetuning requires a high percentage of math and reasoning data like pre-training.
Thinking that math and code tokens naturally make up about 50% of general internet data.

title: Synthetic Data Generation
summary: The use of AI-generated data to increase training data quality and quantity, particularly when human-generated data is limited, expensive, or of lower quality for specific tasks like tool use or complex math.
learning_objective: The learner can explain how synthetic data generation increases data quantity, coverage, and quality, particularly for tasks like tool use or complex math where human data is limited or lower quality.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing synthetic data is always of lower quality than human-generated data, when AI can sometimes exceed human quality for specific tasks.
Assuming synthetic data completely replaces human-generated data, when mixing both often produces the best value.
Thinking synthetic data is only used to increase data quantity, ignoring its role in improving coverage and quality.

title: Transformer Block Architecture
summary: The core building block of foundation models, including self-attention mechanisms and feed-forward layers that determine how the model processes and represents information.
learning_objective: The learner can identify the key components of a transformer block, including self-attention mechanisms and feed-forward layers, and explain how they process information in parallel without RNNs.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing the attention mechanism was introduced with the transformer model rather than three years prior.
Assuming transformers rely on recurrent neural networks for sequential processing instead of parallel token processing.
Thinking the transformer architecture is limited to neural machine translation rather than serving as a general foundation model building block.

title: Model Capacity and Parameter Scaling
summary: How the number of parameters, layers, and hidden dimensions affect model capacity, expressiveness, and the ability to learn complex patterns from data.
learning_objective: The learner can explain how the number of parameters, layers, and hidden dimensions affect model capacity, expressiveness, and the ability to learn complex patterns from data.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that more powerful models require fewer training examples to learn from.
Assuming the number of parameters alone determines memory usage without considering sparsity or precision.
Thinking that increasing parameters always leads to better performance regardless of data quality or quantity.

title: Training Bottlenecks and Resource Constraints
summary: Computational and memory limitations during training, including GPU memory, bandwidth, and the trade-offs between model size and training time.
learning_objective: The learner can identify computational and memory limitations during training, including GPU memory, bandwidth, and the trade-offs between model size and training time.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing GPU memory is the only training bottleneck, ignoring bandwidth and other resource constraints.
Assuming larger models always yield better results without considering training time and resource trade-offs.
Thinking training bottlenecks remain constant throughout the training process rather than shifting between compute, memory, and I/O.

title: Inference Optimization Techniques
summary: Methods for reducing inference latency and cost, such as quantization, caching, and API-based optimizations used in production deployments.
learning_objective: The learner can describe inference optimization techniques at the model, hardware, and service levels, including quantization, distillation, and caching, to reduce latency and cost.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that inference optimization never changes model quality, when many techniques can cause model degradation.
Assuming most application developers implement optimization techniques themselves, when most use model APIs with built-in optimization instead.
Thinking inference service-level optimization changes the model itself, when it typically keeps the model intact and only changes how it is served.

title: Post-Training Workflow
summary: The overall sequence of pre-training, supervised finetuning (SFT), and preference finetuning (e.g., RLHF) used to align a foundation model with user intent.
learning_objective: The learner can describe the post-training workflow consisting of supervised finetuning and preference finetuning used to align a pre-trained foundation model with human preferences.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing post-training adds new knowledge to the model rather than aligning existing capabilities with human preferences.
Assuming post-training consists solely of RLHF, ignoring the supervised finetuning step that precedes preference finetuning.
Thinking post-training makes a model completely safe and foolproof, despite human preference being diverse and impossible to capture in a single formula.

title: Supervised Finetuning (SFT)
summary: Training a pre-trained model on labeled conversational data to convert text-completion behavior into instruction-following dialogue.
learning_objective: The learner can explain how supervised finetuning converts a pre-trained model's text-completion behavior into instruction-following dialogue using labeled conversational data.

common_misconceptions.description: Supervised finetuning can also be used for infilling tasks like text editing and code debugging, not just next-token prediction.
Supervised finetuning can be performed using adapter-based techniques on mid-tier GPUs, not necessarily requiring full finetuning.
Supervised finetuning is often combined with preference finetuning, and steps can be skipped depending on the desired outcome.

title: Preference Finetuning
summary: Aligning model outputs with human preferences using methods such as RLHF, since preferences cannot be captured by a single mathematical formula.
learning_objective: The learner can explain that preference finetuning is a post-training step used to align model outputs with human preferences, which cannot be captured by a single mathematical formula.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that human preferences can be captured by a single mathematical formula.
Thinking preference finetuning is the only step in post-training, ignoring supervised finetuning.
Assuming that a universal human preference exists and can be perfectly embedded into AI.

title: Parameter-Efficient Finetuning
summary: Adapter-based techniques such as LoRA and PEFT that reduce compute and memory requirements compared to full finetuning.
learning_objective: The learner can define parameter-efficient finetuning and explain how adapter-based techniques such as LoRA and PEFT reduce compute and memory requirements compared to full finetuning.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing parameter-efficient finetuning simply means finetuning fewer layers, when it specifically refers to methods that achieve comparable performance with significantly fewer trainable parameters.
Assuming adapter-based techniques have no downsides, even though inserting adapter modules can increase inference latency.
Thinking there is a strict threshold for a method to be considered parameter-efficient, when no clear threshold exists.

title: Finetuning Frameworks and Tactics
summary: Practical tools like LLaMA-Factory, PEFT, and Axolotl, along with tactics such as model merging, multi-task finetuning, and full finetuning.
learning_objective: The learner can identify finetuning frameworks such as LLaMA-Factory, PEFT, and Axolotl and tactics including model merging, multi-task finetuning, and full finetuning.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that finetuning a foundation model always requires updating all model parameters rather than using parameter-efficient methods.
Assuming that because finetuning frameworks simplify the process, obtaining and validating high-quality finetuning data is no longer a challenge.
Confusing model merging with conventional finetuning approaches instead of recognizing it as a distinct experimental technique.

title: Hyperparameter Search Strategies
summary: Methods for exploring the hyperparameter space, including grid search, random search, and Bayesian optimization, to identify configurations that improve model convergence and performance.
learning_objective: The learner can compare grid search, random search, and Bayesian optimization strategies for exploring hyperparameter space to improve model convergence and performance.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing grid search always finds the optimal hyperparameters, ignoring its computational cost and the curse of dimensionality.
Assuming random search is less effective than grid search, when it often finds better configurations with fewer trials.
Thinking Bayesian optimization guarantees finding the global optimum, when it is a probabilistic method that can get stuck in local optima.

title: Learning Rate Scheduling
summary: Techniques for adjusting the learning rate during training, such as warmup, cosine decay, and step decay, to stabilize convergence and improve final model accuracy.
learning_objective: The learner can explain how learning rate schedules adjust learning rates during training to stabilize convergence and improve model accuracy.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that keeping the learning rate constant throughout training is always optimal for convergence.
Assuming that a larger learning rate will always speed up training without causing instability.
Thinking that learning rate scheduling is only necessary for novice practitioners and not for advanced model tuning.

title: Batch Size and Resource Trade-offs
summary: The impact of batch size on training speed, memory usage, gradient stability, and hardware utilization, including how to select batch sizes based on available compute resources.
learning_objective: The learner can explain how batch size affects training speed, memory usage, gradient stability, and hardware utilization, and select appropriate batch sizes based on available compute resources.

common_misconceptions.description: Small batch sizes always lead to unstable training without considering gradient accumulation techniques.
Larger batch sizes always improve hardware utilization without considering memory constraints and diminishing returns.
Batch size only affects training speed and does not impact memory usage or gradient stability.

title: Compute-Optimal Model Scaling
summary: Determining the best model size and dataset size given a fixed compute budget to maximize performance while minimizing cost.
learning_objective: The learner can determine the optimal model size and dataset size for a fixed compute budget to maximize performance using scaling laws.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that arbitrarily increasing model size always yields better performance regardless of compute budget.
Assuming that model quality is the only factor that matters, ignoring production usability and cost constraints.
Thinking the scaling law applies equally to all model types, such as sparse models or those trained on synthetic data.

title: Training Cost vs. Inference Cost Trade-offs
summary: Analyzing the relationship between total training cost and recoverable inference revenue to determine if model development is economically viable.
learning_objective: The learner can determine whether model development is economically viable by comparing total training cost to recoverable inference revenue using the inequality T <= p × N.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing training cost always exceeds inference cost, when inference can account for up to 90% of ML costs in deployed systems.
Assuming third-party API providers can reduce inference cost as usage increases, which does not apply to them selling inference on open source models.

title: Training Data Cost Management
summary: Calculating and managing costs when the acquisition or processing of training data is nontrivial.
learning_objective: The learner can calculate and manage the costs associated with acquiring and processing training data when those costs are nontrivial.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that data labeling costs are constant regardless of dataset size or task complexity.
Assuming that poor data quality does not increase overall project costs by wasting resources.
Thinking that acquiring more data is always beneficial without considering the cost-benefit tradeoff.

title: Difficulty of Evaluating Intelligent Outputs
summary: Explains why evaluating foundation models is harder than traditional ML, as human evaluators struggle to judge high-quality, complex outputs like PhD-level solutions or coherent summaries without deep domain knowledge.
learning_objective: The learner can explain why evaluating foundation models is more difficult than traditional ML, including the need for domain expertise and the lack of comprehensive ground truths for open-ended tasks.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that a response that sounds fluent and coherent is necessarily factually correct or high quality.
Assuming that for every open-ended AI task there is a single, definitive ground truth answer to compare against.
Thinking that any human can reliably judge the quality of complex, expert-level AI outputs without specialized knowledge.

title: Comparative vs. Absolute Performance
summary: Discusses the shift from measuring absolute performance to using comparative evaluation to rank models against each other when absolute ground truth is difficult to establish.
learning_objective: The learner can explain the difference between comparative and absolute performance evaluation and why comparative ranking does not indicate whether a model is good enough for a specific use case.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that a higher comparative win rate directly translates to a specific absolute performance metric, such as ticket resolution rate.
Assuming that if model B ranks higher than model A, model B is automatically good enough for production use.
Thinking there is an absolute ground truth for model rankings when rankings are actually predictive based on historical match outcomes.

title: Lack of Standardization and Quality Control
summary: Addresses the absence of universal standards and quality control mechanisms in foundation model evaluation, making results hard to compare across different studies and providers.
learning_objective: The learner can explain how the absence of universal standards and quality control mechanisms in foundation model evaluation makes results difficult to compare across studies and providers.

common_misconceptions.description: Assuming leaderboard developers can always clearly explain their benchmark selection processes.
Believing that attempts to game evaluation rankings are always admitted or easily detectable.
Thinking all model pairs must be compared an equal number of times to produce a valid ranking.

title: Scalability Bottlenecks in Evaluation
summary: Covers the challenges of scaling evaluation processes due to the high cost and time required for human annotation and testing of large generative outputs.
learning_objective: The learner can identify scalability bottlenecks in evaluation caused by high costs, time requirements, and the lack of standardization in human annotation and testing of large generative outputs.

common_misconceptions.description: Spot-checking is not the same as sampling when evaluating model outputs.
Evaluation can cost more than response generation, sometimes taking up the majority of the budget.
Using powerful models like GPT-4 as AI judges approximately doubles API costs compared to generation alone.

title: Defining Application Requirements
summary: Identifying the specific functional and non-functional needs of an application, such as latency, accuracy, cost, and privacy, to establish the criteria for model selection.
learning_objective: The learner can identify specific functional and non-functional application needs such as latency, accuracy, cost, and privacy to establish criteria for model selection.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that application requirements only include functional capabilities and ignoring non-functional constraints like latency and cost.
Assuming that the same application requirements and criteria apply to all AI applications regardless of their specific use case.

title: Comparing Model Capabilities
summary: Evaluating different foundation models based on their architecture, parameter size, modality support, and general performance characteristics to match them with application needs.
learning_objective: The learner can compare foundation models based on architecture, parameter size, modality support, and performance characteristics to match them with application needs.

common_misconceptions.description: Assuming a model with more parameters always performs better across all tasks.
Believing that high scores on public benchmarks guarantee success in a specific real-world application.
Thinking all foundation models support the same input and output modalities.

title: Evaluating Model Performance
summary: Using benchmarks, evaluation metrics, and comparative testing to determine how well a specific model performs on tasks relevant to the target application.
learning_objective: The learner can evaluate a model's performance using benchmarks, evaluation metrics, and comparative testing to determine its suitability for a target application.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that public benchmarks alone can identify the best model for a specific application.
Confusing comparative evaluation (which model is better) with absolute performance (whether a model is good enough).
Assuming benchmark results are always valid despite potential data contamination in model training sets.

title: Analyzing Cost and Deployment Trade-offs
summary: Assessing the financial and infrastructure implications of using proprietary APIs versus self-hosted open-weight models, including inference costs and scaling requirements.
learning_objective: The learner can compare the financial and infrastructure trade-offs between using proprietary model APIs and self-hosting open-weight models, including token-based inference costs and compute requirements.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that using model APIs is always cheaper than self-hosting, ignoring that high token volume can make API costs exceed compute costs.
Assuming self-hosted models are free because there are no per-token API charges, overlooking the significant cost of compute infrastructure.
Thinking high latency is always a deal breaker for users, when it is often just an annoyance rather than a critical failure.

title: Prompt Engineering
summary: Designing input prompts to guide foundation models toward desired outputs without modifying model weights.
learning_objective: The learner can define prompt engineering as crafting instructions to guide foundation models toward desired outputs without modifying model weights.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing prompt engineering is not a real skill or technique despite its widespread use.
Thinking prompt engineering modifies the model's weights like finetuning does.
Assuming prompt engineering alone is enough to build production-ready AI applications.

title: Fine-Tuning
summary: Updating foundation model weights using task-specific labeled data to adapt behavior for specialized applications.
learning_objective: The learner can define fine-tuning as adapting a foundation model to a specific task by further training its weights using task-specific labeled data.

common_misconceptions.description: Fine-tuning on one task may improve performance for that task but degrade performance on other tasks.
Native fine-tuning is memory-intensive, but techniques like adapter-based methods allow fine-tuning with less memory.
Getting data for fine-tuning is hard, and the amount of data needed depends on the strength of the base model.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation
summary: Combining foundation models with external knowledge retrieval to ground responses in domain-specific data sources.
learning_objective: The learner can define retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) as connecting a foundation model to an external database to supplement instructions and generate better responses.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing RAG is the same as finetuning a model on a dataset rather than supplementing instructions with a database.
Assuming RAG only works with text and cannot be applied to multimodal or tabular data.

title: Defining Evaluation Criteria
summary: Establishing what an application should and should not do, including out-of-scope inputs and expected responses, to avoid ambiguous scoring.
learning_objective: The learner can define evaluation criteria that specify what an application should and should not do, including out-of-scope inputs and expected responses, to avoid ambiguous scoring.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing evaluation criteria only need to describe what the application should do, ignoring out-of-scope inputs and undesired behaviors.
Assuming that vague evaluation guidelines are sufficient because scorers will interpret them consistently.
Confusing the definition of evaluation criteria with the selection of evaluation methods and data.

title: Creating Scoring Rubrics
summary: Developing unambiguous scoring guidelines and examples, including providing scoring reasons, to ensure consistent evaluation by human or AI judges.
learning_objective: The learner can create an unambiguous scoring rubric with examples and scoring reasons, then validate it with humans to ensure consistent evaluation.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that scoring rubrics are optional rather than a critical backbone for reliable evaluation pipelines.
Assuming that a rubric does not need concrete examples of what each score looks like and why.
Thinking that a rubric is ready to use without testing whether humans find it easy to follow.

title: Selecting Evaluation Methods
summary: Choosing appropriate evaluation methods for different criteria, such as toxicity classifiers, semantic similarity, and AI judges for factual consistency.
learning_objective: The learner can select appropriate evaluation methods for different criteria such as toxicity classifiers, semantic similarity, and AI judges for factual consistency.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing a single evaluation method can be used for all criteria instead of matching methods to specific criteria.
Assuming AI judges are always accurate without needing unambiguous scoring rubrics and examples.
Thinking you cannot combine multiple evaluation methods for the same criterion.

title: Domain-Specific Capability Benchmarks
summary: Using public or private benchmarks to evaluate specific capabilities like code generation, math, reasoning, and legal knowledge.
learning_objective: The learner can identify domain-specific benchmarks used to evaluate capabilities such as code generation, math, reasoning, and legal knowledge.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that only public benchmarks exist for evaluating domain-specific capabilities.
Assuming that functional correctness alone is sufficient to evaluate all domain-specific capabilities.

title: Generation Capability Metrics
summary: Evaluating generation qualities such as fluency, coherence, factual consistency, and safety, many of which evolved from traditional NLP.
learning_objective: The learner can identify key generation capability metrics such as fluency, coherence, factual consistency, and safety, and explain how they evolved from traditional NLP metrics like faithfulness and relevance.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that a single set of generation metrics applies equally well to all tasks, ignoring that each task may require its own specific metrics like faithfulness for translation or relevance for summarization.
Assuming that early NLG metrics are no longer used, when in fact many have been repurposed with significant modifications to evaluate foundation model outputs.
Confusing high fluency or coherence with overall generation quality, overlooking other critical dimensions such as factual consistency and safety.

title: Selecting Evaluation Methods
summary: Choosing appropriate evaluation methods such as toxicity classifiers, semantic similarity, and AI judges based on specific criteria, including the use of scoring rubrics and examples for specialized scorers.
learning_objective: The learner can select appropriate evaluation methods for different criteria such as toxicity classifiers, semantic similarity, and AI judges for factual consistency.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing a single evaluation method can be used for all criteria instead of matching methods to specific criteria.
Assuming AI judges are always accurate without needing unambiguous scoring rubrics and examples.
Thinking you cannot combine multiple evaluation methods for the same criterion.

title: Annotating Evaluation Data
summary: The process of labeling and preparing evaluation data, including determining the necessary volume of examples to ensure reliable results without being prohibitively expensive.
learning_objective: The learner can curate a set of annotated examples to evaluate an application's components and criteria using production data, human or AI labeling, and clear scoring rubrics.

common_misconceptions.description: Assuming every application has natural labels that can be used for evaluation without additional labeling effort.
Believing annotation guidelines created for evaluation cannot be reused to create instruction data for finetuning later.
Thinking evaluation sets should be as large as possible without considering cost and reliability trade-offs.

title: Designing Evaluation Data Slices
summary: Creating multiple evaluation sets to represent different data slices, such as production distribution, user tiers, traffic sources, known failure cases, and out-of-scope inputs.
learning_objective: The learner can design multiple evaluation data slices representing production distribution, user tiers, traffic sources, known failure cases, and out-of-scope inputs.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing one evaluation set representing overall production data is sufficient to understand system performance across all scenarios.
Assuming out-of-scope inputs do not need a dedicated evaluation set because the application is not supposed to engage with them.
Thinking the number of examples in each evaluation slice does not matter as long as the data is representative.

title: Creating Evaluation Guidelines
summary: Defining evaluation criteria and creating scoring rubrics with examples to establish clear standards for assessing system outputs.
learning_objective: The learner can create an evaluation guideline that defines what an application should and shouldn't do, including out-of-scope inputs and appropriate responses.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that an ambiguous evaluation guideline is sufficient, which leads to ambiguous and misleading scores.
Thinking evaluation criteria only need to define what the application should do, ignoring what it shouldn't do.
Assuming the application will naturally handle unrelated inputs without explicitly defining out-of-scope detection and response behavior.

title: Evaluating All System Components
summary: Assessing each component of an AI system individually, including domain-specific capability, generation capability, instruction-following capability, cost, and latency.
learning_objective: The learner can evaluate all components of an AI system, including domain-specific capability, generation capability, instruction-following capability, cost, and latency.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that evaluating only the foundation model is sufficient without assessing other system components.
Assuming that capability metrics alone determine system quality while ignoring cost and latency constraints.
Thinking that a single benchmark score can represent all aspects of system performance across different capabilities.

title: Defining Evaluation Methods and Data
summary: Selecting appropriate evaluation methods, annotating evaluation data, and curating test sets that reflect production scenarios including edge cases and out-of-scope inputs.
learning_objective: The learner can select appropriate evaluation methods and curate evaluation data sets that reflect production scenarios, including edge cases and out-of-scope inputs.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing one evaluation set is sufficient to represent all production data slices and edge cases.
Assuming a single evaluation method can measure all criteria without needing specialized scorers or AI judges.
Thinking that specialized scorers and AI judges can succeed without unambiguous scoring rubrics and examples.

title: Tying Metrics to Business Metrics
summary: Connecting evaluation metrics to business outcomes to ensure that technical performance aligns with organizational goals and user needs.
learning_objective: The learner can map technical evaluation metrics to specific business outcomes to ensure system performance aligns with organizational goals.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that metrics themselves are the goal rather than a means to identify problems and improvement opportunities.
Focusing solely on technical performance scores like relevancy without connecting them to business value or user needs.
Overlooking cost-related metrics such as query volume and token usage when tying evaluation to business outcomes.

title: Evaluating and Iterating the Pipeline
summary: Assessing the reliability of the evaluation pipeline itself and iterating on guidelines, methods, and data based on findings to improve evaluation quality over time.
learning_objective: The learner can assess the reliability of an evaluation pipeline and iterate on guidelines, methods, and data based on findings to improve evaluation quality over time.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing public benchmarks alone are sufficient to find the best model for a specific application.
Assuming an evaluation pipeline does not need iteration once it is initially designed.
Thinking evaluation only applies to the final model output rather than all system components.

title: Comparative vs. Absolute Evaluation
summary: Distinguishes ranking models against each other from measuring whether a model is good enough for a specific use case, noting that comparative results alone cannot determine absolute quality.
learning_objective: The learner can explain the difference between comparative and absolute evaluation and identify why comparative results alone cannot determine if a model is good enough for a specific use case.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that if model B beats model A in a ranking, model B is necessarily good enough for production.
Assuming a comparative win rate (e.g., 51%) can be directly converted into an absolute business metric like ticket resolution rate.
Overlooking that a comparative ranking can be valid even when both models being compared are actually bad.

title: Ranking Models via Pairwise Comparisons
summary: Describes how models are evaluated side-by-side to compute a ranking from comparison results, including its use in leaderboards and subjective quality assessment.
learning_objective: The learner can compute a model ranking from historical pairwise match outcomes and use it to predict future match outcomes.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing there is a single ground truth for the correct model ranking rather than a predictive quality measure.
Assuming Bradley-Terry scores are identical to Elo scores without scaling transformations.
Thinking a ranking is reliable for all model pairs regardless of the number of matches observed.

title: Scalability Bottlenecks in Comparative Evaluation
summary: Covers the quadratic growth of model pairs as the number of models increases and the resulting data-intensity challenges for gathering sufficient comparison signals.
learning_objective: The learner can explain why comparative evaluation becomes data-intensive as the number of models increases due to quadratic growth in model pairs.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing the number of comparisons grows linearly with the number of models rather than quadratically.
Assuming that a large total number of comparisons guarantees sufficient signal per model pair.

title: Signal Gathering and Model Ranking Challenges
summary: Addresses difficulties in collecting reliable comparison signals and computing accurate rankings, including the role of human and AI evaluators.
learning_objective: The learner can identify challenges in gathering reliable comparison signals and ranking models, including issues with human and AI evaluators.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing public leaderboards always provide accurate and comparable model rankings.
Assuming human and AI evaluators consistently provide reliable comparison signals without bias.
Thinking there is a single standardized method for evaluating and ranking all foundation models.

title: Absolute vs Comparative Evaluation
summary: Distinguishes absolute evaluation, which measures a model against fixed criteria to determine if it is "good enough" for a specific application, from comparative evaluation, which only ranks models relative to one another.
learning_objective: The learner can distinguish absolute evaluation, which measures a model against fixed criteria to determine if it is "good enough" for a specific application, from comparative evaluation, which only ranks models relative to one another.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that a higher comparative ranking or win rate automatically proves a model is good enough for a specific use case.
Confusing absolute evaluation with finding the best possible model rather than checking if it meets fixed criteria for an application.
Assuming a comparative win rate (e.g., 51%) can be directly converted into an absolute performance metric like ticket resolution rate.

title: Domain-Specific Capability Evaluation
summary: Evaluates specialized skills such as code generation, math, and reasoning using domain-specific benchmarks, focusing on functional correctness and exact evaluation methods.
learning_objective: The learner can evaluate domain-specific capabilities using exact evaluation methods such as functional correctness and efficiency metrics.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing functional correctness is the only aspect that matters when evaluating domain-specific capabilities.
Confusing exact evaluation with general generation capability evaluation like fluency or coherence.

title: Generation Capability Evaluation
summary: Assesses the quality of generated text using language modeling metrics like perplexity and similarity measurements against reference data when automatic evaluation is possible.
learning_objective: The learner can assess generation capabilities using language modeling metrics such as perplexity and similarity measurements against reference data.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that lower perplexity always indicates higher quality generated text.
Assuming high similarity to reference data guarantees factual consistency.
Thinking automatic evaluation metrics alone are sufficient to assess all generation capabilities.

title: Instruction-Following Evaluation
summary: Measures how well a model adheres to user constraints and guidelines using scoring rubrics, examples, and defined evaluation criteria.
learning_objective: The learner can define instruction-following capability and explain how scoring rubrics, examples, and defined evaluation criteria are used to measure how well a model adheres to user constraints.

common_misconceptions.description: Instruction-following failure is often confused with a lack of domain-specific knowledge or generation capability.
Poor model performance is assumed to be the model's fault without considering that the instruction itself may be bad.
Instruction following is treated as a strict pass/fail rather than a partial score based on meeting multiple criteria.

title: System-Level Cost and Latency Evaluation
summary: Evaluates non-functional requirements such as efficiency, runtime, memory usage, and cost to determine if a model's performance is practical for real-world deployment.
learning_objective: The learner can calculate system-level cost and latency for model deployment by analyzing compute cost, throughput, token usage, and the impact of parallelism strategies.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing high latency is always a deal breaker when it is often just an annoyance.
Assuming pipeline parallelism reduces latency when it actually increases total latency due to communication overhead.
Thinking higher throughput increases cost when it typically lowers cost per token.

title: Evaluation Pipeline Design
summary: Outlines the end-to-end process for building an evaluation system, including creating guidelines, defining methods and data, annotating evaluation sets, and iterating based on results.
learning_objective: The learner can outline the end-to-end process for building an evaluation system, including creating guidelines, defining methods and data, annotating evaluation sets, and iterating based on results.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that public benchmarks alone are sufficient to find the best model for a specific application.
Assuming that more evaluation data is always better without considering cost and reliability trade-offs.
Thinking that evaluation pipeline design is a one-time linear process rather than an iterative cycle.

title: Limitations of Comparative Evaluation
summary: Comparative rankings do not reveal absolute performance; a model can win against another while both are bad, both good, or one good and one bad, making it unclear if a swap is worthwhile.
learning_objective: The learner can explain why comparative rankings do not reveal absolute performance and why a model win does not guarantee a worthwhile swap.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that a higher comparative win rate directly indicates a model is good enough for a specific use case.
Assuming that knowing which model is better tells you how good either model actually is.
Thinking that any model that wins a comparison should replace the current model without further evaluation.

title: Scalability Bottlenecks in Comparative Evaluation
summary: Comparative evaluation is data-intensive because the number of model pairs grows quadratically with the number of models, requiring large numbers of comparisons for reliable rankings.
learning_objective: The learner can explain why comparative evaluation becomes data-intensive as the number of models increases due to quadratic growth in model pairs.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing the number of comparisons grows linearly with the number of models rather than quadratically.
Assuming that a large total number of comparisons guarantees sufficient signal per model pair.

title: Lack of Standardization and Quality Control
summary: Challenges in ensuring consistent and reliable evaluation signals when using human or AI judges, including variability in voter quality and the need for evaluation guidelines and rubrics.
learning_objective: The learner can explain how the absence of universal standards and quality control mechanisms in foundation model evaluation makes results difficult to compare across studies and providers.

common_misconceptions.description: Assuming leaderboard developers can always clearly explain their benchmark selection processes.
Believing that attempts to game evaluation rankings are always admitted or easily detectable.
Thinking all model pairs must be compared an equal number of times to produce a valid ranking.

title: Domain-Specific Capability Benchmarks
summary: Using public or private benchmarks to assess capabilities such as math, science, reasoning, code generation, and tool use.
learning_objective: The learner can identify domain-specific benchmarks used to evaluate capabilities such as code generation, math, reasoning, and legal knowledge.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that only public benchmarks exist for evaluating domain-specific capabilities.
Assuming that functional correctness alone is sufficient to evaluate all domain-specific capabilities.

title: Generation Quality Criteria
summary: Evaluating fluency, coherence, factual consistency, faithfulness, and safety of model outputs.
learning_objective: The learner can define fluency, coherence, factual consistency, faithfulness, and safety as criteria for evaluating the quality of generated text outputs.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that grammatically correct and natural-sounding text is necessarily factually correct.
Confusing local grammatical fluency with the global logical structure of a text.
Assuming faithfulness applies only to translation and not to tasks like summarization.

title: Instruction-Following and Scope
summary: Defining what an application should and should not do, including out-of-scope input detection and response behavior.
learning_objective: The learner can define instruction-following capability and explain how to measure whether a model's output meets all specified criteria for an instruction.

common_misconceptions.description: Confusing a model's failure to follow an instruction with a lack of domain-specific knowledge or generation capability.
Assuming a model successfully follows an instruction if it meets some, but not all, of the specified criteria.
Believing that poor model performance is always due to the model itself rather than the quality of the instructions provided.

title: Operational Evaluation Factors
summary: Assessing cost, latency, and other operational metrics alongside quality criteria.
learning_objective: The learner can assess cost, latency, and other operational metrics alongside quality criteria when evaluating AI systems.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that evaluation should focus solely on output quality while ignoring operational factors like cost and latency.
Assuming operational metrics are secondary considerations rather than core criteria that must be assessed alongside quality.

title: Evaluation Methods and Scoring Rubrics
summary: Selecting methods such as classifiers, semantic similarity, and AI judges, and creating unambiguous scoring guidelines with examples.
learning_objective: The learner can select appropriate evaluation methods such as classifiers, semantic similarity, and AI judges for different criteria and create unambiguous scoring rubrics with examples.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing a single evaluation method can be used for all criteria without considering the specific nature of each criterion.
Assuming that scoring rubrics and examples are optional when using AI judges or specialized scorers.
Thinking that only one evaluation method can be applied to a single criterion rather than mixing and matching methods.

title: Build Versus Buy Decision
summary: Evaluating whether to develop a custom foundation model in-house or procure an existing model via API or open weights based on cost, control, and time-to-market.
learning_objective: The learner can evaluate whether to build a custom foundation model in-house or buy an existing model via API or open weights by comparing cost, control, and time-to-market.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that building a model in-house is always cheaper than paying for model providers, ignoring that provider prices can drop and make in-house the expensive option.
Assuming that investing in a third-party solution is safe, without considering the risk that the provider could go out of business.
Thinking that adapting an existing model is as difficult as building one from scratch, when it can be significantly easier and faster.

title: Navigating Public Benchmarks
summary: Using public leaderboards and benchmarks to compare candidate models while understanding the limitations and opacity of benchmark selection processes.
learning_objective: The learner can use public benchmarks and leaderboards to filter out bad models while recognizing benchmark limitations such as data contamination and opaque selection processes.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing public benchmarks can identify the best model for a specific application rather than just filtering out bad ones.
Assuming leaderboard benchmark selection and aggregation processes are always transparent and easily explainable.
Thinking benchmark data is isolated from model training sets and therefore free from contamination.

title: Resolving Conflicting Benchmark Results
summary: Applying decision criteria when candidate models show contradictory performance across different benchmarks for the same task domain.
learning_objective: The learner can apply decision criteria to select a model when candidate models show contradictory performance across different benchmarks for the same task domain.

common_misconceptions.description: Assuming all benchmarks measure the same capability equally, ignoring that benchmarks like TruthfulQA are only moderately correlated with reasoning benchmarks.
Believing a model that performs best on one benchmark is superior overall, without considering contradictory results on other benchmarks in the same domain.
Thinking that simply averaging benchmark scores resolves conflicting results, when averaging treats all benchmarks equally and may mask important performance trade-offs.

title: Evaluate All System Components
summary: Assessing every part of an AI application, not just the model, to ensure each component functions correctly within the system.
learning_objective: The learner can assess every part of an AI application, not just the model, to ensure each component functions correctly within the system.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that evaluating only the model is sufficient for system success.
Assuming public benchmarks alone can identify the best model for a specific application.

title: Create Evaluation Guidelines
summary: Defining scoring rubrics with examples and tying evaluation criteria to business metrics to standardize assessment.
learning_objective: The learner can create an evaluation guideline that defines what an application should and shouldn't do, including out-of-scope inputs and corresponding responses.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that an ambiguous evaluation guideline is sufficient because scores will naturally be consistent.
Assuming that defining only what the application should do is enough, without specifying how to handle out-of-scope inputs.
Thinking that evaluation criteria alone are sufficient without providing concrete examples of good and bad responses.

title: Define Evaluation Methods and Data
summary: Selecting appropriate evaluation methods, annotating data, and determining the necessary volume of examples for reliable results.
learning_objective: The learner can define evaluation methods and data by selecting appropriate evaluation methods for different criteria, annotating evaluation data, and slicing data to represent different production slices.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that one evaluation method can be used for all criteria instead of mixing and matching methods like classifiers, semantic similarity, and AI judges.
Thinking a single evaluation set is sufficient rather than having multiple sets to represent different data slices and production distribution.
Assuming evaluation can proceed without annotated data when humans or AI may be needed to label examples if natural labels are unavailable.

title: Evaluate and Iterate the Pipeline
summary: Assessing the evaluation pipeline itself for cost, latency, and metric correlation, then iterating based on findings.
learning_objective: The learner can assess an evaluation pipeline for cost, latency, and metric correlation and iterate based on findings.

common_misconceptions.description: Skipping evaluation reduces latency and cost without negative consequences.
If two metrics are perfectly correlated, you don't need both of them.
Public benchmarks will help you find the best models for your application.

title: Prompt Fundamentals
summary: Defines what a prompt is, its key components such as system prompt, user prompt, examples, and context, and how prompt engineering guides model behavior without changing weights.
learning_objective: The learner can define a prompt and identify its key components such as system prompt, user prompt, examples, and context.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing a prompt consists only of the user's question rather than the whole input including system instructions and context.
Thinking that prompt engineering modifies the model's internal weights instead of guiding behavior through input.

title: Prompt Engineering Best Practices
summary: Covers techniques for writing effective prompts, including crafting detailed instructions, providing examples, systematic testing, versioning prompts, and standardizing evaluation metrics.
learning_objective: The learner can apply prompt engineering best practices such as crafting detailed instructions, providing examples, systematically testing changes, versioning prompts, and standardizing evaluation metrics.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing prompt engineering is not a real skill or technique despite it being a common model adaptation method.
Thinking prompt engineering is the only skill needed to build production-ready AI applications, ignoring statistics, engineering, and ML knowledge.
Relying on superficial tricks like promising a tip or using shorthand labels instead of systematic best practices for effective prompts.
Assuming a prompt that improves a model's performance on a subtask will necessarily improve the performance of the whole system.

title: Prompt Engineering Tools
summary: Discusses tools that assist with prompt engineering, such as those for structured outputs and prompt variation, along with risks like hidden API calls and unnecessary costs.
learning_objective: The learner can identify prompt engineering tools for structured outputs and prompt variation and explain the risks of hidden API calls and unnecessary costs.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing prompt engineering tools do not generate hidden model API calls that can quickly increase costs.
Assuming prompt engineering tools will not change their prompt templates or default prompts without warning.
Thinking that using prompt engineering tools removes the need to inspect generated prompts or understand the underlying model.

title: Prompt Attacks and Defense
summary: Covers how to defend AI applications against prompt attacks as part of building production-ready systems.
learning_objective: The learner can identify common prompt attack approaches and apply defensive techniques such as instruction hierarchy and defensive prompt engineering to protect AI applications.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that because security is an evolving cat-and-mouse game, no effective defenses against prompt attacks exist.
Assuming tool outputs have the highest priority in instruction hierarchy, when they actually have the lowest priority.
Thinking repeating the system prompt twice has no drawbacks, ignoring the increased cost and latency from extra tokens.

title: RAG Architecture
summary: The two-component structure of a RAG system consisting of a retriever that fetches information from external memory sources and a generator that produces responses based on retrieved information.
learning_objective: The learner can describe the two-component structure of a RAG system consisting of a retriever that fetches information from external memory sources and a generator that produces responses based on retrieved information.

common_misconceptions.description: RAG modifies the underlying model weights to incorporate new information.
RAG is limited to text-based data sources only.
RAG completely eliminates model hallucinations.

title: RAG vs Finetuning
summary: Guidance on choosing between RAG and finetuning based on whether model failures are information-based (factual errors, outdated knowledge) or behavior-based, and how they can be combined.
learning_objective: The learner can distinguish between information-based and behavior-based model failures to decide whether to apply RAG, finetuning, or a combination of both.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing RAG is only useful for factual knowledge and cannot help with behavioral issues like output formatting.
Thinking finetuning is the best way to add new factual information to a model rather than adjusting its behavior or format.
Assuming RAG and finetuning cannot be used together in the same application.
Believing you must start with vector databases for RAG instead of simpler term-based solutions like BM25.

title: RAG Evaluation
summary: Factual consistency as a key evaluation criterion for RAG systems, measuring whether generated responses align with retrieved context from external databases.
learning_objective: The learner can explain factual consistency as a key evaluation criterion for RAG systems by describing how generated responses should align with retrieved context from external databases.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that evaluating the retriever alone (e.g., with NDCG or MAP) is sufficient to assess the factual consistency of the final generated response.
Assuming that adding RAG automatically guarantees factually consistent outputs without needing specific evaluation of consistency between context and generation.
Thinking that human expert baselines like the 94% on TruthfulQA are not relevant reference points for evaluating RAG factual consistency.

title: RAG Implementation Starting Points
summary: Practical recommendations for beginning RAG implementations, including starting with simple term-based solutions like BM25 before adopting vector databases, and when full context inclusion may eliminate the need for RAG.
learning_objective: The learner can identify simple term-based solutions like BM25 as the recommended starting point for RAG implementations before adopting vector databases.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that vector databases are the necessary first step for any RAG implementation.
Assuming RAG and finetuning are mutually exclusive and cannot be used together.

title: Agent Definition and Core Concepts
summary: Defines an agent as an entity that perceives its environment through sensors and acts upon it through actuators, distinguishing agentic patterns from simple retrieval by enabling autonomous action-taking and decision-making.
learning_objective: The learner can define an agent as an entity that perceives its environment through sensors and acts upon it through actuators, distinguishing agentic patterns from simple retrieval by enabling autonomous action-taking and decision-making.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that an agent is simply a RAG system rather than an entity capable of autonomous action and decision-making.
Assuming there are established theoretical frameworks for defining, developing, and evaluating AI-powered agents.
Thinking an agent can perform any action regardless of its specific actuators and environment constraints.

title: Agent Tools
summary: Covers the external capabilities and interfaces that agents use to interact with the world, extending model functionality beyond text generation to include API calls, code execution, and other action-taking mechanisms.
learning_objective: The learner can identify and categorize external tools that extend an agent's capabilities beyond text generation, such as knowledge augmentation, capability extension, and environment interaction tools.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that providing more tools always improves agent performance, when in fact too many tools can make it harder for the agent to understand and utilize them effectively.
Assuming tool selection is independent of the AI model, when the choice of tools depends heavily on the specific model powering the agent.
Thinking that giving an agent tools removes the need for planning or reasoning, when tools are capabilities that must be selected and invoked within a multi-step agentic workflow.

title: Agent Planning
summary: Explores how agents decompose tasks, sequence actions, and make autonomous decisions to solve complex problems, representing the cognitive layer that directs tool usage toward goal completion.
learning_objective: The learner can describe how an agent decomposes a task into a plan, sequences actions, and makes autonomous decisions to achieve a goal within constraints.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that generating a plan is the same as executing it, ignoring the separate validation and execution stages.
Assuming agents always plan independently without any human involvement in generating, validating, or executing plans.
Thinking that any decomposed plan will lead to a successful outcome, rather than recognizing that some decompositions are more efficient or correct than others.

title: Agent Failure Modes
summary: Discusses the new modes of failure introduced by agentic operations, including error propagation in multi-step reasoning, tool misuse, and infinite loops, which differ from standard generation failures.
learning_objective: The learner can identify agent failure modes caused by planning, tool execution, and efficiency, and explain how they differ from standard generation failures.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing agent failures are limited to standard AI generation errors rather than including planning, tool execution, and efficiency issues.
Assuming tool failures are the same across all tools instead of being tool-dependent and requiring independent testing.
Thinking the time an agent takes to complete a task is irrelevant even when deadlines make timeliness critical.

title: Memory Systems
summary: Memory systems manage and utilize information that exceeds the maximum context length of the underlying model, supporting both RAG and agent applications.
learning_objective: The learner can describe how memory systems manage information exceeding a model's maximum context length to support RAG and agent applications.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that a model's internal knowledge changes with every query rather than only when the model is updated.
Assuming that short-term memory (context) persists across different tasks or queries when it does not.
Thinking FIFO is the only memory management strategy, ignoring retention of N last messages or tokens.

title: Agent Security Risks
summary: Tool use exposes agents to security risks that require rigorous defensive mechanisms for real-world deployment, as automated agents can have catastrophic failures.
learning_objective: The learner can identify security risks introduced by tool use in agents and explain why rigorous defensive mechanisms are required for real-world deployment.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing agent failures are limited to technical bugs rather than including catastrophic security risks from tool use.
Assuming defensive mechanisms are optional add-ons instead of rigorous requirements for real-world agent deployment.

title: When to Finetune
summary: Criteria for deciding whether to finetune versus using prompt-based methods, considering resource requirements in data, hardware, and ML talent.
learning_objective: The learner can determine whether to finetune a model or use prompt-based methods by evaluating data, hardware, and ML talent requirements.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing finetuning should be the first approach tried before experimenting with prompt engineering.
Assuming finetuning requires fewer resources than prompt-based methods.
Thinking that starting with a less refined model reduces the effort needed to adapt it to a specific task.

title: Full Finetuning
summary: The approach of training all model parameters, where the number of trainable parameters equals the total number of parameters, typically used when models are small enough.
learning_objective: The learner can define full finetuning as training all model parameters where the number of trainable parameters equals the total number of parameters.

common_misconceptions.description: Full finetuning starts with previously trained weights, not randomized weights like training from scratch.
Full finetuning uses all parameters, not a subset like partial finetuning or parameter-efficient methods.

title: Adapter-Based Finetuning
summary: Parameter-efficient finetuning techniques that allow adapting models with less memory, often requiring only a mid-tier GPU, supported by frameworks like PEFT and LLaMA-Factory.
learning_objective: The learner can explain how adapter-based finetuning works by inserting trainable adapter modules into transformer layers while keeping original model parameters frozen, and identify its trade-offs in parameter efficiency versus inference latency.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing adapter-based finetuning updates all model weights when it actually keeps original parameters unchanged and only updates adapter parameters.
Assuming adapter-based finetuning has no inference overhead when it actually increases inference latency due to the inserted adapter modules.
Thinking adapter-based finetuning needs the same memory as full finetuning when it uses far fewer trainable parameters and can run on mid-tier GPUs.

title: Finetuning Frameworks and Compute
summary: Overview of finetuning frameworks such as LLaMA-Factory, unsloth, Axolotl, and LitGPT, and compute provisioning options ranging from local GPUs to cloud integration.
learning_objective: The learner can compare full finetuning and adapter-based finetuning in terms of compute requirements and identify frameworks such as LLaMA-Factory, PEFT, and Axolotl for each approach.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing adapter-based finetuning is always faster than full finetuning regardless of model size or dataset.
Assuming all finetuning frameworks support identical methods and hardware configurations without trade-offs.
Thinking a mid-tier GPU is sufficient for full finetuning of most foundation models.

title: Data and Memory Considerations
summary: Challenges of obtaining finetuning data and calculating model memory footprint, including memory bottlenecks that make native finetuning memory-intensive.
learning_objective: The learner can calculate the memory footprint of a model during finetuning by accounting for weights, optimizer states, and gradients based on parameter count and numerical format.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that only the model weights need to be stored in memory during finetuning, ignoring optimizer states and gradients.
Assuming that all parameters must be trainable for finetuning, overlooking partial finetuning techniques that reduce memory requirements.
Confusing model storage size with the active memory required for backpropagation and training.

title: Data Quality
summary: Ensuring data is accurate, reliable, and free from errors, analogous to using fresh ingredients in cooking, as poor data can cause model biases and hallucinations.
learning_objective: The learner can define data quality in model training and explain how high-quality data impacts model performance compared to noisy data.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that a larger volume of training data always leads to better model performance regardless of noise or relevance.
Assuming that data quality does not significantly affect model performance as long as the data quantity is sufficient.

title: Data Coverage
summary: Ensuring the dataset has the right mix of diverse usage patterns and characteristics to represent all necessary scenarios without over- or under-representing specific types.
learning_objective: The learner can explain data coverage as the criterion ensuring training data includes the right mix of domains and topics without over- or under-representing any area.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing data coverage is about the total amount of data rather than the diversity and balance of domains and topics.
Confusing data coverage with data quality, which concerns the correctness and reliability of individual examples rather than the mix of data.

title: Data Quantity
summary: Determining the appropriate volume of data required for training, balancing the need for sufficient examples against resource constraints.
learning_objective: The learner can explain how data quantity is determined by balancing training costs, desired capabilities, and the specific situation, recognizing that required amounts range from single examples to trillions of tokens.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that more data always leads to better performance regardless of quality or diversity.
Assuming there is a single fixed amount of data required for all models and tasks.
Thinking data quantity matters more than data quality and coverage for model performance.

title: Data Filtering and Deduplication
summary: The process of removing low-quality samples and duplicate entries from raw data to build a clean dataset foundation.
learning_objective: The learner can identify and remove low-quality samples and duplicate entries from raw data using heuristics and deduplication techniques.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that only exact text matches count as duplicates, ignoring near-duplicates or paraphrased content.
Assuming that lists with the same items in different orders are not duplicates.
Thinking that deduplication must always happen before filtering low-quality data, regardless of efficiency.

title: Overlap Analysis
summary: Analyzing the intersection between different data subsets to prevent data leakage and ensure distinct training, validation, and test sets.
learning_objective: The learner can identify overlapping data across training, validation, and test sets using overlap estimation techniques such as Bloom filters to prevent data leakage.
