common_misconceptions.description: Believing that overlap analysis only detects exact duplicates rather than partial matches like 80% overlap.
Assuming overlap analysis only applies at the document level and ignores paragraph, sentence, or token-level duplications.
Thinking that two lists with the same items in different order are not considered duplicates.

title: Data Quality Dimensions
summary: Defining data quality for finetuning using dimensions such as completeness, uniqueness, validity, accuracy, consistency, and fitness for purpose.
learning_objective: The learner can list and define the data quality dimensions of completeness, uniqueness, validity, accuracy, consistency, and fitness for purpose as they apply to finetuning datasets.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that a larger volume of data automatically results in higher data quality for model finetuning.
Assuming that the same set of data quality dimensions applies equally to all use cases without considering the specific context of finetuning.

title: Annotation Consistency
summary: Ensuring annotations are consistent across examples and annotators to avoid confusing the model during training.
learning_objective: The learner can explain why annotations must be consistent across examples and annotators to avoid confusing the model during training.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that accurate annotations are sufficient even if they differ between annotators.
Assuming small differences in annotations between annotators won't affect model learning.
Thinking that items receiving the same score are necessarily of the same quality.

title: Annotation Guidelines and Fact-Checking
summary: Creating annotation guidelines, updating them based on feedback, and fact-checking annotations to correct factual errors.
learning_objective: The learner can create annotation guidelines aligned with task requirements, update them based on feedback, and fact-check annotations to correct factual errors.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing annotation guidelines do not need updates after initial creation.
Assuming annotations are inherently factually correct without a fact-checking step.
Confusing consistent annotations across annotators with factually accurate annotations.

title: Data Cleaning and Filtering
summary: Removing extraneous formatting tokens, PII, sensitive data, copyrighted data, and toxic content to ensure dataset safety and performance.
learning_objective: The learner can remove extraneous formatting tokens, PII, sensitive data, copyrighted data, and toxic content from a dataset to ensure safety and performance.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that leaving HTML tags in training data does not affect model accuracy or token length.
Assuming data should always be cleaned before filtering or deduplication, regardless of computational cost.
Thinking it is safe to modify the original dataset directly without keeping a backup copy.

title: Manual Data Inspection
summary: Manually inspecting data to verify annotation trustworthiness, check example uniqueness, and identify inconsistencies.
learning_objective: The learner can manually inspect annotated data by sampling examples, self-annotating to compare with given labels, fact-checking responses, and identifying duplicate queries with conflicting responses to assess annotation trustworthiness.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that data exploration tools can fully replace the need to manually stare at and inspect raw data.
Assuming that provided annotations are correct without verifying them by attempting to annotate the same examples yourself.
Thinking that all examples in a dataset are unique and not checking for the same query appearing with different responses.

title: Reasons for Synthesizing Data
summary: Explores the motivations behind generating synthetic data, including scaling training sets, addressing data scarcity, and improving model performance across different training phases.
learning_objective: The learner can explain the reasons for synthesizing data, including increasing data quantity, improving coverage and quality, mitigating privacy concerns, and enabling model distillation.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing synthetic data completely replaces human-generated data rather than complementing it.
Thinking data synthesis is only used to increase quantity, ignoring coverage, quality, privacy, and distillation.
Assuming synthetic data is always lower quality than human-generated data when it can sometimes exceed it.

title: Traditional Data Synthesis Techniques
summary: Covers rule-based methods and simulation-based approaches for generating synthetic data without relying on AI models.
learning_objective: The learner can describe traditional data synthesis techniques, including rule-based methods and simulation-based approaches, for generating synthetic data without AI models.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that synthetic data generation always requires AI models or machine learning.
Confusing rule-based data synthesis with simulation-based approaches, treating them as identical techniques.

title: AI-Powered Data Synthesis
summary: Describes the use of foundation models to generate instruction data and other synthetic examples, including template-based generation and model distillation.
learning_objective: The learner can explain how foundation models are used to generate synthetic instruction data through template-based generation and model distillation.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing synthetic data completely replaces human-generated data rather than complementing it.
Thinking data synthesis is only for increasing data quantity, ignoring coverage, quality, privacy, and distillation use cases.

title: Data Verification Methods
summary: Focuses on techniques for verifying synthetic data quality, such as programmatic verification through code execution and back-translation.
learning_objective: The learner can describe programmatic verification methods for synthetic data, including code execution and back-translation.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that programmatic verification guarantees data quality rather than just checking specific properties.
Assuming all synthetic data can be programmatically verified when some data cannot be verified this way.
Thinking verification alone is sufficient without additional data curation steps like filtering and cleaning.

title: Limitations of Synthetic Data
summary: Discusses challenges associated with AI-generated data, including model collapse, quality control issues, and superficial imitation problems.
learning_objective: The learner can identify key limitations of synthetic data, including model collapse, quality control challenges, and superficial imitation issues.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing synthetic data is always of lower quality than human-generated data, when sometimes the reverse can be true.
Assuming synthetic data completely replaces human-generated data, when mixing both often produces the best value.
Thinking evaluation of synthetic data is straightforward, when it remains challenging and ultimately depends on real-world performance.

title: Data-Centric Benchmark Competitions
summary: Competitions that evaluate dataset quality by training models on submitted datasets and measuring performance on standardized downstream tasks, such as CLIP model training and language model benchmarks.
learning_objective: The learner can explain how data-centric benchmark competitions evaluate dataset quality by training models on submitted datasets and measuring performance on standardized downstream tasks.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing the competition evaluates the model architecture rather than the quality of the dataset used to train it.
Assuming dataset quality is measured by a single task rather than performance across multiple standardized downstream tasks.
Thinking participants use their own training scripts instead of a standardized script provided by the competition.

title: DataPerf and dcbench
summary: Standardized data-centric benchmarks from MLCommons and academic research used to assess dataset quality through model performance metrics.
learning_objective: The learner can explain how DataPerf and dcbench serve as standardized data-centric benchmarks that assess dataset quality through model performance metrics.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing these benchmarks measure model architecture performance rather than dataset quality.
Assuming DataPerf is the only standardized data-centric benchmark and ignoring dcbench.

title: Downstream Task Evaluation
summary: Assessing dataset quality by measuring the performance of models trained on the dataset across multiple downstream tasks rather than intrinsic dataset properties.
learning_objective: The learner can assess dataset quality by measuring model performance across multiple downstream tasks rather than relying on intrinsic dataset properties.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that intrinsic dataset properties alone are sufficient to determine dataset quality without downstream task evaluation.
Assuming that performance on a single downstream task is representative of overall dataset quality across multiple tasks.

title: Inference Performance Metrics
summary: Key metrics used to evaluate inference speed and cost, including latency, throughput, and cost per prediction.
learning_objective: The learner can define latency, throughput, and goodput as key metrics for evaluating inference speed and cost.

common_misconceptions.description: Confusing throughput with goodput, ignoring that goodput only counts requests meeting service level objectives.
Believing latency is the sole performance indicator, overlooking throughput and cost per prediction.

title: AI Accelerators
summary: Hardware-level optimization using specialized processors such as GPUs and TPUs to run inference faster on target hardware.
learning_objective: The learner can define an AI accelerator as a chip designed to accelerate AI workloads and identify GPUs as the dominant type.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing CPUs and GPUs serve the same general-purpose role rather than GPUs being specialized for parallel workloads.
Assuming accelerators are only for training rather than also being used for faster inference on target hardware.

title: Model Optimization
summary: Model-level techniques to reduce a trained model's size or develop more efficient architectures to improve speed and cost.
learning_objective: The learner can describe model-level inference optimization techniques such as quantization and distillation and explain how they reduce model size or improve efficiency.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing model-level optimization never alters model behavior, when techniques like quantization can change model outputs.
Assuming most application developers implement optimization techniques themselves, when most use model APIs with built-in optimization.
Thinking inference optimization happens only at the model level, ignoring hardware and service-level approaches.

title: Inference Service Optimization
summary: Service-level optimization that refines the entire inference process, including serving infrastructure and request handling.
learning_objective: The learner can describe how inference service optimization refines the entire inference process, including serving infrastructure and request handling, while keeping the model intact.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing inference service optimization changes the model itself, when it typically only changes how the model is served.
Thinking service-level optimization only covers request handling, ignoring that it also refines serving infrastructure and the entire shooting process.

title: Simplest Foundation Model Application Architecture
summary: The baseline architecture for a foundation model application, consisting of a model and a user interface, serving as the starting point before adding complexity.
root: AI Engineering Architecture and User Feedback
learning_objective: The learner can describe the baseline architecture of a foundation model application consisting of a model and a user interface.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing the simplest architecture requires additional components like vector databases or agents.
Thinking a foundation model application can function without a user interface.

title: Challenges of Simple AI Application Architectures
summary: The limitations and failure modes encountered when using only the simplest architecture, which motivate the addition of further components.
root: AI Engineering Architecture and User Feedback
learning_objective: The learner can identify the limitations and failure modes of simple AI application architectures that motivate the addition of further components.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that the simplest architecture is sufficient for all AI applications without considering its limitations.
Assuming that simple AI architectures do not have specific failure modes that require additional components to address.

title: Incremental Component Addition for AI Products
summary: The gradual approach of adding engineering components to address specific challenges and build more successful AI applications.
root: AI Engineering Architecture and User Feedback
learning_objective: The learner can describe the gradual approach of adding engineering components to address specific challenges and build more successful AI applications.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that all AI engineering components must be implemented simultaneously rather than incrementally.
Assuming that every AI application requires the same set of engineering components regardless of its specific challenges.

title: User Feedback in AI Product Evaluation
summary: The process of putting an application in front of users to gather feedback and determine whether it achieves its intended goals.
root: AI Engineering Architecture and User Feedback
learning_objective: The learner can explain how putting an application in front of users to gather feedback determines whether it achieves its intended goals.

common_misconceptions.description: Believing that acting on user feedback always improves the product, when it can actually create degenerate feedback loops that amplify biases.
Thinking that reasoning about how to build a successful application is enough, without putting it in front of users to gather actual feedback.
